sketches: Reversing a single arc is a locally finite perturbation, and for tournaments an induced copy of T is a subtournament copy. So Conjecture 24 supplies, for every non-transitive finite tournament H, a countable H-free tournament in which any single arc reversal creates H, answering Problem 23 for all non-transitive H (the transitive cases are handled by known finite examples noted in the paper).

Reversing a single arc is a locally finite perturbation, and for tournaments subtournament containment equals induced containment; so the source's S_T witnesses that every non-transitive T belongs to the class the target asks to characterize (transitive T are excluded in the infinite setting by Ramsey).

source.name: Induced-saturated infinite tournament existence
source.statement: Let $T$ be a finite tournament. If $T$ is not transitive, then there exists a countably infinite $T$-free tournament $S_{T}$ such that every locally finite perturbation of $S_{T}$ has an induced copy of $T$.
source.context: This is proposed as the tournament analogue of the paper's main Theorem 1. The non-transitivity condition is necessary because any tournament on $2^n$ elements contains a transitive subtournament on $n$ elements, so a transitive $T$ cannot be avoided in an infinite structure under locally finite perturbations.

target.name: Arc-reversal induced saturation in tournaments
target.statement: For which finite tournaments $H$, does there exist a countable tournament $G$ that does not contain $H$ as subtournament, yet any tournament obtained from $G$ by changing the direction of a single arc does contain $H$?
target.context: The authors ask for a tournament analogue of induced saturation, where the natural perturbation operation is reversing arcs. They note that when $H$ is a directed triangle there is no finite $G$ but an infinite one exists (the rationals ordered by $<$), and that for the transitive tournament on 3 elements a finite example exists.

sketches: Forcing implies Sidorenko (standard, also in the directed setting: the forcing property is defined via the Sidorenko-type inequality with equality only for quasirandom targets). Bipartite oriented B with a homomorphism to K-vec2 either has a cycle in its underlying graph (then Conjecture 1.7 gives forcing, hence Sidorenko) or is a forest, for which the directed Sidorenko property is easy/known.

source.name: Directed forcing characterization via homomorphism
source.statement: If $B$ is an oriented graph with a homomorphism to an edge and whose underlying undirected graph has a cycle, then $B$ has the directed forcing property.
source.context: Theorem 1.6 establishes that admitting a homomorphism to a directed edge and having a cycle in the underlying undirected graph are both necessary conditions for the directed forcing property. The authors conjecture these two conditions together are also sufficient, providing a directed analogue of the Skokan–Thoma forcing conjecture.

target.name: Directed Sidorenko property for K₂-homomorphic bipartite
target.statement: If $B$ is a bipartite oriented graph with a homomorphism $B \to \vec{K}_2$, then $B$ has the directed Sidorenko property.
target.context: Observation 3.1 establishes that having a homomorphism to a directed edge is a necessary condition for the directed Sidorenko property. The authors conjecture this condition is also sufficient for bipartite oriented graphs, giving a directed analogue of Sidorenko's conjecture.

sketches: Problem 2.15 asks for the full complexity classification of circular F-colourability over all fixed F; Conjecture 2.16 is the assertion resolving the cyclic-F half of that dichotomy (NP-completeness whenever F contains a directed cycle; acyclic F are trivially polynomial). Solving the classification problem settles the conjecture.

source.name: Circular F-colourability complexity dichotomy
source.statement: Let $F$ be a fixed (multi-)digraph. Instance: A (multi-)digraph $D$. Decide whether $D$ is circularly $F$-colourable.
source.context: A digraph $D$ is circularly $F$-colourable if there exists a circular homomorphism from $D$ to $F$. This problem generalises Problem 1 and serves as a directed analogue of the $H$-colouring problem for graphs. Conjecture 2.16 asserts that NP-completeness holds whenever $F$ contains a directed cycle, and Theorem 2.17 establishes this for almost all such cases.

target.name: NP-completeness of circular F-coloring
target.statement: Let $F$ be a digraph which contains a directed cycle. Then the circular $F$-colouring problem is NP-complete.
target.context: The authors conjecture that, under the assumption $\mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}$, the only polynomially solvable instances of Problem 2.15 are those where $F$ is acyclic (for which only acyclic digraphs map circularly to $F$). Theorem 2.17 confirms this conjecture for almost all cases.

sketches: The question whether every orientation of C4 is Eulerian-avoidable is the instance of the general characterization problem 'which digraphs are Eulerian-avoidable' restricted to the four orientations of the 4-cycle; a full characterization answers it.

source.name: Characterization of Eulerian-avoidable digraphs
source.context: A digraph $F$ is Eulerian-avoidable if there exists $d_F:\mathbb{N}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}$ such that every Eulerian digraph (where each vertex has equal out- and in-degree) with minimum out-degree at least $d_F(k)$ contains an $F$-free subdigraph with minimum out-degree at least $k$. This setting is highlighted as potentially yielding new insights complementing the regular digraph characterization proved in the paper.

target.name: C₄ Eulerian-avoidability in orientations
target.context: Restricting to Eulerian digraphs (where each vertex has equal out- and in-degree) may make avoidability questions more tractable. The authors ask whether the specific case of $C_4$, which is open in the general setting, becomes resolvable in the Eulerian host digraph setting.
